title: Face pareidolia: why does that house look surprised?
description: Two windows and a doorway can suddenly look like a face. Discover face pareidolia, the everyday illusion that gives ordinary objects a personality.

cover.alt: A cream miniature house with two square windows above an arched doorway, suggesting a surprised face
cover.credit: AI-generated conceptual illustration created for BrainiLab, using ordinary windows and a doorway to suggest a face.

practice: Keep spotting patterns with a round of Odd One Out.

sources.name: UNSW Sydney (2020) — Why the brain is programmed to see faces in everyday objects
University of Sydney (2021) — Why our brains see human faces everywhere

sections.title: Is that house looking at you?
sections.html:
Two upstairs windows. An open doorway below. Suddenly, the house looks surprised to see you.

Face pareidolia is seeing a face in something that is not one, such as a building, a tree trunk or a cloud. It is one kind of pareidolia: finding a recognisable pattern in something ambiguous. The face is your interpretation of the object’s features.

sections.title: A familiar arrangement
sections.html:
Human faces vary, but their features follow a familiar arrangement. Two eye-like shapes above a mouth-like shape can be enough to suggest a face.

UNSW researchers tested face-like objects and found evidence that they recruit some of the same visual mechanisms used to read where human faces are looking. A pair of windows can make quite an impression.

sections.title: Why does the tree look grumpy?
sections.html:
We can read an expression into the pattern, too. A University of Sydney study mixed real faces with face-like objects and asked people to judge their expressions. Similar biases appeared in both kinds of judgment.

Knowing it is a tree does not necessarily make the apparent face disappear. You can recognise the object and still see the scowl. The tree has not developed an opinion about your shoes.

sections.title: Give the ordinary a second look
sections.html:
A building’s windows remain windows. The extra character comes from how we see them.

If perception has caught your curiosity, try the colour-word mix-up called the Stroop effect. Or explore another everyday surprise: where flamingos get their pink colour. Familiar things have plenty left to tell us.
